entries.title: Claude found 493 attack-surface issues in 25 projects; OpenSSH made ML-DSA parsing unreachable before auth
entries.summary: Anthropic ran Claude over 25 open-source projects (over five million lines) to find code reachable without need, rather than individual bugs. It found 493 issues, including 94 configuration combinations that silently turned off a security control, and a pattern in four projects where hostname-based deny rules fail open when reverse DNS lookups are off. In OpenSSH, about 4,500 lines of ML-DSA-44 post-quantum code were reachable before authentication even when the algorithm was disabled; after several rounds of fixes, OpenSSH 10.6 checks the allow lists before parsing.

lessons.point: Option combinations are a large blind spot: many were accepted silently and undocumented.
lessons.excerpt: Claude found 162 security sensitive configuration combinations that were accepted both without an error or warning and without any documentation of the expected behavior of their interaction.

lessons.point: sshd parsed attacker-chosen key types before checking whether they were allowed.
lessons.excerpt: The daemon parsed whichever key type the client sent, (and, for certificates, it also verified the embedded CA signature). Only then did it check whether that key type was allowed.

lessons.point: Hostname deny rules compared against a bare IP never match, so the list fails open.
lessons.excerpt: This means that a deny rule would never fire, and the list would fail open.

lessons.point: For the default-configuration pass, a gate is accepted only when the project's own tests give identical results.
lessons.excerpt: it requires modified builds to have identical results.

entries.takeaway: Cutting pre-auth and default-reachable code lowers the severity of bugs you have not found, and an LLM can do this audit at scale.

actionable.title: Run a three-pass attack-surface reduction review with an LLM
actionable.detail: In fresh contexts, have the model (1) inventory entry points reachable in the default config that no intended feature uses, (2) list parsing or state recorded before auth or protocol state transitions, and (3) enumerate security-relevant option pairs that silently disable or weaken a control; confirm each with a dynamic trace, and accept a gate only if the project's test suite gives identical results.

entries.prior_art: Pool entries on frontier-model vulnerability discovery (Mythos-era bug finding, AI-built PHP pre-auth chains) and classic attack-surface reduction guidance; this shifts from finding individual bugs to systematic reachability and config-interaction reduction with measured results and an upstream OpenSSH fix. Verifier: Attack-surface reduction (Howard/Manadhata attack-surface metrics, OpenSSH privsep and pre-auth minimization) is classic, and Anthropic's prior LLM vuln-finding posts (Firefox, OSS-Scanner) cover LLM bug finding. What is new is LLM-driven reachability and config-interaction auditing at scale, with the concrete OpenSSH 10.6 pre-auth fix.
entries.verify_note: Independent fresh-context verifier re-read the source; the overstatements it flagged were corrected before merge.
entries.threat: Complex, memory-unsafe or security-sensitive code reachable by unauthenticated clients, and configuration combinations that silently disable controls administrators believe are on.
entries.conditions: Default configurations exposing unused features, checks that run after parsing, and option pairs accepted without warnings, such as hostname deny rules with reverse DNS off or certificate requirements dropped by a conflicting option.
entries.mitigations: Upgrade OpenSSH to 10.6; check allow lists before deserialization; reject conflicting security options at config load; use IP-based access rules or enable DNS lookups when using hostname rules.

entries.title: PwnEscape: pwn.ai used an LLM research harness to find a new Linux networking bug class that escapes KVM guests (CVE-2026-99999)
entries.summary: pwn.ai researchers, working in Vercel's sandbox challenge, found that guest-controlled checksum metadata can rewrite an IPv4 header after the host kernel has validated it. The bug is in Linux networking, not in KVM itself, so many hypervisors are affected. In their lab they turned a memory disclosure into selected 64-byte host-kernel writes and a host-root helper run. They credit GPT-5.6 Sol as the main reasoning engine inside a long-running research harness. The upstream fix validates checksum_start before completing the checksum.

lessons.point: The authors call it a new class: untrusted checksum metadata edits packet fields after validation.
lessons.excerpt: untrusted checksum metadata can rewrite security-sensitive packet fields after the kernel has already validated and acted on them

lessons.point: The bug is outside the hypervisor, so KVM-only audits miss it.
lessons.excerpt: the vulnerability wasn't even in the hypervisor, it was in the Linux networking stack.

lessons.point: An LLM provided source-level analysis within a human-directed harness.
lessons.excerpt: served as the primary reasoning engine for source-level analysis, exploring attack paths, and challenging assumptions

lessons.point: The accepted fix validates the checksum start.
lessons.excerpt: ipv4: validate checksum_start before completing checksum

entries.takeaway: VM isolation depends on the kernel's networking code, so patch KVM hosts and sandbox providers.

actionable.title: Patch hypervisor hosts and sandbox providers
actionable.detail: Apply the kernel fix on every KVM host (and nested or microVM sandboxes), and ask your sandbox provider for their patch status; treat guest-originated packet metadata as untrusted in custom kernels.

entries.prior_art: Earlier VM-escape work targets hypervisor device emulation; this reaches the host through guest-controlled metadata in core networking, with LLM-assisted discovery. Verifier: Checksum offload/virtio_net metadata bugs (virtio-net GSO/csum handling fixes); Google Big Sleep and XBOW LLM-driven vuln finds; kvmCTF KVM escapes

entries.title: Claude wrote machine-checked no-crash proofs for 239 OSS-Fuzz entry points across 123 libraries at the RISC-V binary level by turning fuzz harnesses into specs
entries.author: Keane Lucas et al. (Anthropic, Theorem)
entries.summary: Anthropic and Theorem had Claude prove, in Rocq, that 239 OSS-Fuzz entry points in 123 open-source libraries never crash (no memory-safety error or failed assertion) for any input up to 64 MB, after patching the bugs it found along the way. The spec is derived mechanically from the existing fuzz harness plus formal RISC-V and Linux-process semantics, so the ~180M lines of proof need no human review: trust reduces to the semantics, the theorem statements and the Rocq checker. Scope is narrow (single-threaded static RISC-V binaries, fixed memory budget) and compute is large, but it moves formal verification from niche to a pipeline step.

lessons.point: LLM-written formal proofs now scale to production libraries at the binary level, not just toy programs.
lessons.excerpt: proved that there are no crashes on any input (up to 64 MB) for 239 entry points across 123 different OSS-Fuzz libraries

lessons.point: The spec problem is sidestepped by reusing what developers already wrote: an existing fuzz harness becomes the property to prove.
lessons.excerpt: automatically converting their preexisting compilable test suites into a spec

lessons.point: Machine checking replaces review of the AI output: the trusted base is the semantics, the theorem statements and the checker, not the 600k-line proofs.
lessons.excerpt: virtually none of it needs to be manually reviewed

lessons.point: The guarantee is scoped: it holds only for single-threaded static RISC-V binaries on Linux under a memory budget, and bugs may remain in the trusted components.
lessons.excerpt: assume that the program runs as a single-threaded static binary with a fixed memory budget on a RISC-V CPU using Linux OS

lessons.point: Attempting proofs is itself a bug finder: failures pointed at real bugs that fuzzing had missed.
lessons.excerpt: the process of attempting to prove these specs discovered hundreds of bugs

entries.threat: AI-accelerated bug discovery and exploit chaining outpacing test-based assurance for memory-unsafe code.
entries.conditions: C/C++ libraries with existing fuzz harnesses; proofs currently limited to single-threaded static RISC-V Linux binaries.
entries.mitigations: Turn fuzz harnesses into no-crash specs and have an LLM produce checker-verified proofs; review the theorem statements and trusted semantics rather than proof text.
entries.takeaway: If you maintain C/C++ with fuzz harnesses, those harnesses are now candidate proof specs: an LLM plus a proof checker can turn 'fuzzed a lot' into 'proved no crash' for the covered scope.

actionable.title: Fuzz-harness-to-proof pipeline
actionable.detail: For a C/C++ library already in OSS-Fuzz, try Theorem's published add-project Claude skill and pipeline on one entry point; review only the generated theorem statement and assumptions, and treat proof failures as bug reports.

entries.prior_art: seL4 and CompCert (human-written verification at 10x code effort), binary-level verifiers like Alive2, LLM proof assistants (Baldur, AlphaProof), and AI bug finding (Big Sleep, AIxCC). None showed LLM-written, machine-checked binary-level proofs at this scale.
entries.verify_note: Independent verifier: all excerpts verbatim; novelty 78 vs 75 (kept 75); relevance 72; noted trusted components may hold bugs and the compute cost is large.

entries.title: PHP2Shell: Wiz used frontier AI to turn memory-safety bugs in core PHP (two CVEs) into unauthenticated RCE on WordPress, Drupal and Joomla
entries.summary: Wiz Research reported memory-safety bugs in the PHP engine itself (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, up to CVSS 9.2), so every PHP version back to 5.4 is hit by at least one of them. The bugs sit in how PHP handles fatal errors such as out-of-memory, so a hello-world app is exposed. The bugs had existed for years; frontier models made the multi-step exploit chain practical to build and adapt per target in hours. PHP shipped the patch on October 21, 2026.

lessons.point: The bugs are in core PHP, so every app on an affected version is exposed, including a plain Hello World app.
lessons.excerpt: Every PHP version released in the last decade is affected by at least one of these vulnerabilities, going back to version 5.4.

lessons.point: The root cause is stale internal state left behind after fatal errors such as out-of-memory, which a later request or worker reuses.
lessons.excerpt: All of the disclosed vulnerabilities are memory-safety issues that stem from bugs in how PHP handles fatal errors while processing requests, particularly out-of-memory errors.

lessons.point: Frontier models made the exploit chain practical: they adapted exploits to different targets in hours.
lessons.excerpt: Frontier models were critical to making this process practical, enabling us to develop and adapt working exploits across multiple applications in hours.

lessons.point: Exploit complexity may no longer be a reliable barrier, so old memory bugs deserve faster patching.
lessons.excerpt: As the time and expertise required for this work decrease, complexity may no longer provide a meaningful barrier, changing how we define what is vulnerable in practice.

entries.takeaway: Patch PHP now: the flaws are in the engine, not your app, and AI has cut the cost of turning old memory bugs into working exploits.

actionable.title: Patch PHP and inventory PHP runtimes
actionable.detail: Upgrade every PHP runtime to the October 21, 2026 release, including PHP bundled in container images. If you cannot patch yet, apply your WAF or CDN vendor's PHP2Shell rule as a stopgap and treat memory disclosure as a credential-rotation trigger on exposed hosts.

entries.prior_art: Core-language RCE disclosures exist (for example PHP-CGI), but a core PHP memory-corruption chain exploited pre-auth across three CMSs with frontier-model-built exploits has no equal in the pools. Verifier: Google Big Sleep / Project Zero AI-found bugs, DARPA AIxCC, XBOW; earlier frontier-model exploit-development reports. Delta is AI-built multi-bug chain on core

entries.title: Microsoft: China-aligned Storm-0940 used the agentic ARTEX pentest framework to hit 2,250+ tenants after the ConnectWise supply-chain compromise
entries.summary: Microsoft says Storm-0940 used ARTEX, an open-source multi-agent penetration-testing framework, to run password spraying, reconnaissance and OAuth-application abuse at machine speed after the ConnectWise Cloud Backup compromise. The actor tried to sign in to more than 2,250 tenants, and in several cases went from first targeting to privileged cloud access in under 3 hours. Most attempts failed, but the speed left defenders little time to respond.

lessons.point: Agentic tooling is already used by a state-aligned actor to scale known tradecraft such as spraying and OAuth abuse.
lessons.excerpt: ARTEX is an open-source penetration testing framework that can use any AI model to automate a variety of offensive security workflows.

lessons.point: Time to privileged cloud access fell under 3 hours in several cases.
lessons.excerpt: Several of these Storm-0940 ARTEX-driven attacks have resulted in the actor obtaining privileged access to an organization’s cloud infrastructure – including multiple instances where the time from initial targeting to privileged access was less than 3 hours.

lessons.point: Alerts fire, but the pace outruns coordinated response.
lessons.excerpt: the speed of the activity allows very little time for Defenders to respond to those alerts and remediate the actor’s access in a coordinated fashion.

lessons.point: Hunt for service-principal sign-ins and unexpected credential or privilege changes on applications.
lessons.excerpt: Customers should review service principal sign-ins, investigate unexpected application credential or privilege changes

entries.takeaway: Agent-driven intrusions compress the time from first touch to privileged cloud access to hours, so detection and OAuth-app hygiene must work at machine speed.

actionable.title: Audit OAuth apps and service principals
actionable.detail: List enterprise apps and service principals with tenant-wide consent, review recent credential additions and privilege changes through Microsoft Graph, and alert on bursts of sign-in failures per minute. Rehearse a response that assumes hours, not days.

entries.title: ITRES Labs used ChatGPT to rebuild two BruCON Windows kernel techniques, whose source was never released, in about 24 hours
entries.summary: A researcher with no recent kernel experience used ChatGPT, conference slide photos, Git history and a compiled executable to rebuild two Windows kernel execution-redirection techniques shown at BruCON 2026. The original author had spent about four months on them and never released source. Both techniques reached SYSTEM on Windows 11 with VBS (virtualization-based security), HVCI (hypervisor-protected code integrity) and kernel shadow stacks enabled, after about 24 hours of recorded work. The model refused 39 times and broke working code late in the project, so the last integration step was finished by hand.

lessons.point: Partial public material (slides, Git history, a compiled binary) was enough to reconstruct unreleased techniques with LLM help.
lessons.excerpt: Using public research, Git history and a compiled executable, we went on to reconstruct and reproduce two of his techniques: Native SSDT and Shadow SSDT.

lessons.point: The author argues researchers should rethink how hard it is for others to weaponize partial disclosures.
lessons.excerpt: But the assumptions about how difficult it is for someone else to turn partial published information into custom working code may no longer be valid.

lessons.point: Model refusals were frequent but inconsistent: it helped build similar functionality earlier, then refused the final integration.
lessons.excerpt: That is approximately 13.8% of the 282 final assistant responses.

lessons.point: Offline test harnesses validated parsing logic only; real kernel effects needed a protected Windows lab with A/B/A restore checks.
lessons.excerpt: They didn’t prove that we could modify kernel execution, restore the original state or obtain a SYSTEM identity.

entries.takeaway: The author argues LLMs make partially disclosed exploit research much cheaper to reproduce, so release decisions for talks, binaries and repos should assume others can rebuild it.

actionable.title: Treat released binaries and slides as reproducible source
actionable.detail: Before publishing exploit research, assume a compiled PoC, slide photos and Git history can be turned into working code by an LLM-assisted non-expert within days. Scrub binaries and history you do not intend to release (deleting a repo late does not undo earlier clones), and plan defender guidance (detections, patches) to land with the talk, not after.

entries.prior_art: Closest pool work covers frontier AI agents compressing intrusion timelines (archive: 'Frontier AI Agents Compress a Two-Week Intrusion Into 10 Hours') and LLM research harnesses finding bugs (PwnEscape); this adds a measured case of LLM-assisted reproduction of unreleased kernel exploitation research from partial artifacts, plus refusal counts. Verifier: Earlier work showed LLMs speeding up exploit reproduction from partial information (e.g., GPT-4 one-day exploitation from CVE descriptions, Fang et al. 2024; AI-assisted n-day patch-diff reproduction). This adds a concrete kernel/HVCI case study with refusal counts, but the thesis itself is not new.
entries.verify_note: Independent fresh-context verifier re-read the source; the overstatements it flagged were corrected before merge.
entries.threat: Attackers with modest expertise can rebuild unreleased exploitation techniques from conference talks, deleted repos and compiled PoCs using general-purpose LLMs.
entries.conditions: Partial technical material is public (slides, Git history, a compiled executable); the reproduced techniques still require administrator privileges to load or use the tooling.
entries.mitigations: Researchers: avoid publishing compiled PoCs or history you do not intend to release; coordinate defensive guidance with disclosure. Defenders: keep VBS/HVCI enabled and monitor for vulnerable driver loading and admin-to-kernel paths.

editorial.reason: tl;dr sec-featured case of an LLM-assisted researcher rebuilding Windows kernel techniques from slides and a binary in about 24 hours; it changes how to weigh partial disclosure.

entries.title: Unit 42: ransomware groups try PAN-OS CVE-2026-0257 to bypass GlobalProtect MFA, and one case pivoted to vCenter and ESXi

entries.title: Citizen Lab: AdFection, zero-click Candiru spyware delivered through targeted ads bought via Discover-Tech

entries.title: Sentry's Next.js tunnelRoute skipped middleware for everything under the tunnel path, not just the requests its rewrite served (GHSA-mchm-gjx6-7h55)
entries.summary: @sentry/nextjs's tunnelRoute option forwards browser events through a path on your own Next.js server and tells the SDK to skip middleware for them. The skip matched every path under the tunnel prefix, while the rewrite only served the exact tunnel path with the o and p parameters, so any app route that resolves under that prefix (a direct collision or a root dynamic segment like app/[locale]) ran without middleware. It is only an authorization bypass where middleware is the sole authz layer; fixed in 9.47.2, 10.75.2 and 11.0.0-rc.1.

lessons.point: The bug is a scope mismatch: an exemption (skip middleware) was matched more broadly than the thing it existed to protect (the rewrite).
lessons.excerpt: The middleware skip was wider than the rewrite.

lessons.point: Requests in the gap reach application routes with middleware never executed.
lessons.excerpt: Requests in that gap go to your application instead of Sentry, and your middleware never runs on them.

lessons.point: It is only exploitable when middleware is the sole authorization layer for the colliding routes; server-side session checks still hold.
lessons.excerpt: your middleware is the only place that enforces authorization for those routes

lessons.point: The durable fix is defense in depth: enforce authorization in the route, layout or data-access layer as well as middleware.
lessons.excerpt: Enforce authorization in the route, layout or data-access path as well as in middleware.

lessons.point: Only webpack builds are affected.
lessons.excerpt: Turbopack builds are not affected

entries.threat: Unauthenticated access to Next.js routes whose only authorization check lives in middleware, by requesting them under the Sentry tunnel prefix.
entries.conditions: tunnelRoute set; webpack build; an app route resolving under the tunnel path (including a root dynamic segment); middleware-only authorization.
entries.mitigations: Upgrade @sentry/nextjs to 9.47.2 / 10.75.2 / 11.0.0-rc.1; move tunnelRoute to a path no route can resolve under; build with Turbopack; enforce authz in routes or data access, not only middleware.
entries.takeaway: Any SDK or framework that exempts paths from middleware is a potential authz bypass: if middleware is your only authorization check, grep your dependencies for middleware skips.

actionable.title: Audit middleware exemptions and add route-level authz
actionable.detail: Upgrade @sentry/nextjs; then list every matcher/skip that bypasses Next.js middleware (Sentry tunnel, static assets, health checks) and confirm each protected route also checks the session server-side in its layout, route handler or data-access layer.

entries.prior_art: Next.js CVE-2025-29927 (x-middleware-subrequest middleware bypass) established that middleware-only authorization in Next.js is fragile; this is a new, SDK-introduced instance of the same class.
entries.verify_note: Independent verifier: all excerpts verbatim; novelty 40 (same); stressed the route-collision precondition and that server-side session checks still protect routes.

editorial.reason: Critical GHSA in a ubiquitous Next.js SDK with a transferable lesson: middleware exemptions are authz bypasses wherever middleware is the only authorization check.

entries.title: 38.9% of agent-generated PRs carry a security smell - but humans introduce most of the real leaked secrets
entries.author: A H M Nazmus Sakib et al.
entries.summary: A large-scale study of the AIDev dataset classified security smells across 16,112 file changes in 4,022 agent-generated pull requests. 38.9% of agent PRs contain at least one security smell and supply-chain integrity issues make up 82.3% of them - but the counterintuitive result is that human collaborators introduce 67.6% of the genuine leaked secrets in these agent-assisted workflows, and review catches almost none of them. All percentages are downstream of an LLM-as-a-judge classification pipeline plus manual review, so treat the precision of the figures accordingly.

lessons.point: Supply-chain integrity dominates the detected smell taxonomy (82.3%); the abstract does not enumerate the remaining categories, so everything else combined is a small residual - point provenance and dependency controls at agent output.
lessons.excerpt: 38.9% of agent-generated PRs contain at least one security smell, with supply chain integrity issues accounting for 82.3% of all detected security smells

lessons.point: Blaming the agent misreads the data: humans introduced most genuine leaked secrets, which the authors describe only as suggesting a *potential* reduction in developer vigilance - an association, not a causal finding.
lessons.excerpt: human collaborators are responsible for introducing 67.6% of genuine leaked secrets within these agent-assisted workflows

lessons.point: Existing review is not a control here - automated and human review together missed 81.1% of these credentials before integration.
lessons.excerpt: existing automated and human review processes fail to detect 81.1% of these credentials prior to integration

entries.threat: Security debt accumulates in high-impact file paths faster than human review capacity, with hard-coded credentials making up 99.6% of critical-severity smells.
entries.conditions: Repositories that accept autonomous coding-agent pull requests through a conventional human review process.
entries.mitigations: Enforce secret scanning as a merge gate rather than a review step; apply provenance/dependency-integrity checks to agent PRs; add context-aware guardrails at the human-AI collaboration point rather than at final review.
entries.takeaway: Gate agent PRs with automated secret and dependency-integrity checks - human review demonstrably does not catch this class, and the humans are introducing most of it.
entries.prior_art: That LLM-generated code contains vulnerabilities is well documented (Copilot-era studies onward). The delta is scale and attribution on real agent PRs - the 67.6% human-origin secrets finding inverts the 'the agent is the risk' framing. Methodologically it applies an existing technique (LLM-as-judge + manual coding) to a new dataset rather than introducing a new method. Accepted at the KDD 2026 AgenticSE workshop.
entries.verify_note: Independent verifier: removed invented contrast categories (injection/logic bugs); restored the authors' 'potential' hedge on developer vigilance; surfaced that all figures come from an LLM-as-a-judge pipeline; novelty 68->57.

editorial.reason: Large-scale, widely-discussed finding on coding-agent risk with a concrete gate: automated secret + dependency-integrity scanning on agent PRs, because human review misses 81%.

entries.title: OVHcloud CLI: attacker swapped binaries on five GitHub releases for 94 minutes, delivering the GlassWorm loader
entries.summary: An attacker replaced the binaries on five OVHcloud CLI GitHub releases, kept them live for 94 minutes, then deleted the evidence. StepSecurity rebuilt the attacker's build, recovered the GlassWorm loader from an orphaned commit, and ran the full chain in isolation. Their replay shows the install.sh script never served arm64 Linux, Homebrew was not an infection path, and running the CLI's version command was enough to spot the malicious build.

lessons.point: Release assets can be swapped after publication and the evidence deleted, so a short exposure window can leave few traces.
lessons.excerpt: An attacker swapped the binaries on five OVHcloud CLI releases, stayed live for 94 minutes, and deleted the evidence.

lessons.point: Deleted malicious code could still be recovered from an orphaned commit, which made a full detonation possible.
lessons.excerpt: recovered the GlassWorm loader from an orphaned commit, and detonated the full chain in an isolated chamber

lessons.point: Exposure depends on install channel: Homebrew was not affected, and a simple version check identifies the bad build.
lessons.excerpt: Homebrew was never a path in, and a single ovhcloud version command was enough to spot the malicious build

entries.takeaway: Release binaries can be replaced after publication, so pin and verify checksums or provenance for downloaded CLIs instead of trusting the release tag.

actionable.title: Triage OVHcloud CLI installs and verify release-asset integrity

entries.prior_art: Closest pool entry is the LiteLLM 1.107.0 trojanized PyPI/Docker release (built from a lookalike repo); release-asset swaps on GitHub are a known vector, but the reconstructed detonation and per-channel exposure analysis are new. entries.mitigations: Check the installed build with `ovhcloud version`; reinstall from a known-good release; pin checksums or verify provenance for release-asset downloads; restrict and monitor release-edit permissions.

entries.title: How we found 24 Android vulnerabilities using our open source AI security agent
entries.summary: GitHub Security Lab extended its open-source Taskflow Agent with Android-specific audit steps. One taskflow separates mobile from non-mobile entry points, and another checks a fixed list of vulnerability classes against each entry point. Together they found 24 vulnerabilities, including OsmAnd location tracking and a WebView account-takeover chain. The post is candid that LLMs over-report low-severity bugs, misjudge severity, and need PoC runs plus expert review.

lessons.point: Give the model a per-entry-point checklist of vulnerability classes so non-determinism doesn't skip the essential bug classes on less familiar platforms like Android.
lessons.excerpt: Since mobile application vulnerabilities are less widely known and LLMs are non-deterministic, we should ensure the LLM checks for certain essential vulnerabilities classes.

lessons.point: Run a strict checklist prompt several times alongside a broad open-ended prompt: the first catches the obvious bugs and the second finds the creative ones.
lessons.excerpt: By combining both prompts across multiple runs, we get the best of each

lessons.point: LLM auditors over-report low-impact or unrealistic-state bugs, even when told not to, so every finding needs expert triage.
lessons.excerpt: it often reported low-severity vulnerabilities, even when specifically told not to do so

lessons.point: Making the model write a proof of concept surfaces mitigating factors it otherwise misses; a debugger is the stronger fix for the false positives that remain.
lessons.excerpt: the only way to fix these issue is to give the LLM a debugger to run the proof of concept and original code

entries.takeaway: Scaffolded, platform-specific taskflows make LLMs effective Android bug hunters, but severity and exploitability still need a PoC and a human.

actionable.title: Two-stage Android audit: classify entry points, then checklist per entry point
actionable.detail: Stage 1: enumerate exported activities, services, receivers, deeplinks and JS bridges, and separate mobile from non-mobile entry points. Stage 2: for each entry point, prompt for its class-specific checklist (intents: confused deputy, insecure broadcast; WebView: XSS, exposed bridges; files: path traversal). Run that strict pass several times plus one open-ended pass, then require a PoC for every finding before human triage.

entries.prior_art: Earlier GHSL Taskflow Agent posts on generic audit taskflows, and LLM-assisted SAST triage; the delta is the Android-specific entry-point and checklist decomposition plus its field results.

entries.title: Google: eight eMudhra intermediate CA keys had weak entropy, so Chrome blocked them within two hours and is removing the root
entries.summary: On October 17, 2026 Google's Chrome Root Program got a report that private keys for eight eMudhra subordinate CA certificates were generated with insufficient randomness, which would let anyone forge trusted HTTPS certificates. entries.title: 333 Tor exit relays hijacked with the Ebury backdoor to intercept SSH passwords and unencrypted mail
entries.summary: A researcher who goes by kaba found that attackers had taken over about 333 Tor exit relays (roughly 10% of exits) and set them to redirect SSH on port 22 to 12 interception servers, stealing passwords, watching sessions and infecting the real server with Ebury. They had gained access to the servers in August and deployed Ebury 1.8.3 on them. Tor's network health team flagged the relays as bad exits on October 4 and all were offline by October 5. The attack also favored unencrypted mail traffic.

lessons.point: SSH on port 22 was silently redirected to attacker servers on infected exits.
lessons.excerpt: if you attempt an SSH connection over Port 22, you're unknowingly redirected to one of 12 SSH interception servers.

lessons.point: The infection started two months earlier with a Linux credential-stealing backdoor.
lessons.excerpt: The attackers had gained access to the servers two months earlier, in August, and quietly deployed their Ebury 1.8.3 payload (an OpenSSH backdoor and credential stealer for Linux).

lessons.excerpt: To give you a sense of scale, all of Tor has around 3000 exit relays, so roughly 10% were under their control.

entries.title: A few notes on AWS Nitro Enclaves: KMS integration
entries.summary: Trail of Bits enumerates passive and active attack classes against the Nitro Enclave to AWS KMS communication channel: encryption-context omission, CMK substitution, attestation-request replay, and the fact that TLS to KMS terminates outside the HSM. They also flag an end-to-end verifiability gap: even with immutable key policies, AWS Support can restore default policies for a key owner, so there is no Certificate-Transparency-style public log a third-party client can independently verify.
entries.takeaway: Enclave-to-KMS attestation only closes the gap if you also hardcode the CMK ARN, attest the IAM role, and initiate TLS from inside the enclave; without that, active-attacker equivalence returns.

lessons.point: Attestation documents are not cryptographically bound to KMS requests, so a captured attestation is replayable for five minutes against any supported operation with attacker-chosen parameters.
lessons.excerpt: As attestations are not cryptographically bound to the requests, the attacker can use the attestation with any supported operation with arbitrary params.

lessons.point: KMS terminates TLS outside the HSM, so end-to-end confidentiality between the enclave and the HSM is not achievable and AWS insiders belong in the threat model.
lessons.excerpt: KMS terminates TLS outside of HSM ([most likely](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/cryptographic-details/internal-communication-security.html)), and the attestation's pubkey encryption is probably done outside of HSM. This makes it impossible to have an end-to-end TLS channel between enclave and HSM, and AWS insiders may theoretically constitute an active attacker threat.

lessons.point: Even immutable key policies do not deliver true end-to-end verifiability, because AWS Support can restore a default policy on the owner's request and there is no public append-only log a third party can audit.
lessons.excerpt: Note that key owners can always [contact AWS support to restore default key policies]... However, we are not aware of any "Certificate Transparency"-style public, append-only log for KMS key policies that an external party can independently verify.

lessons.point: The official aws-nitro-enclaves-sdk-c is C code that Trail of Bits found host-exploitable and recommends avoiding in favor of a Rust NSM library plus Boto3 for KMS.
lessons.excerpt: Amazon ships a lot of SDKs for various tasks. Among them is [`aws-nitro-enclaves-sdk-c`](https://github.com/aws/aws-nitro-enclaves-sdk-c) that provides tools and a library for enclaves-KMS communication. Avoid it: this particular SDK is written in C, and we found it contains vulnerabilities that can be used to exploit enclaves from the parent host.

actionable.title: Enclave-KMS hardening checklist
actionable.detail: For any enclave-KMS integration: hardcode CMK ARN (attested), attest the IAM role via sts:GetCallerIdentity, initiate TLS from inside the enclave with a pinned Amazon CA, use encryption contexts that the host cannot fully control, and monitor kms:PutKeyPolicy externally since AWS Support can restore default policies.

entries.prior_art: No direct pool entry; the Trail of Bits Nitro Enclaves attack-surface post is cited in this piece but not indexed. Standing claims do not cover KMS-enclave attestation replay.
entries.threat: A privileged host or malicious insider between enclave and KMS can swap ciphertexts, substitute CMKs, replay attestations, or bypass immutable key policies via AWS Support restoration.
entries.conditions: Applies when a Nitro Enclave uses KMS with attestation-based key access, does not initiate its own TLS to KMS, or uses key aliases instead of full CMK ARNs.
entries.mitigations: Bundle KMS CA cert inside the enclave and pin it; initiate TLS from within the enclave; attest full CMK ARN and IAM role; use encryption contexts under enclave control; deny kms:PutKeyPolicy globally; alarm on key deletion; publish a client-visible policy monitor. Prefer aws-nitro-enclaves-nsm-api (Rust) + Boto3 over aws-nitro-enclaves-sdk-c (C).

entries.title: Pillow GHSA-w889-685w-c8fh: attacker-controlled filenames inject Ghostscript arguments in EPS handling, even with -dSAFER
entries.summary: The advisory reports that Pillow's EPS plugin builds the Ghostscript command line from the input file's name with no sanitization. A filename starting with '-' is read by Ghostscript as an option, and '@' triggers its argument-file syntax, so an attacker who controls the filename passed to Image.open can inject arguments that chain to command execution. Pillow's default -dSAFER does not stop it. The full command-execution chain also needs an attacker-controlled argument file. Tested on 12.3.0; the suggested fix is to normalize the path to an absolute path.

lessons.point: The fix is to normalize the path so it can never parse as an option.

entries.title: Wiz scans every new npm version at publish time with diffing, sandboxed execution and an AI classifier to catch compromises pre-CVE
entries.summary: Wiz describes a pipeline that analyzes each new npm package version as soon as it is published. In the keyv compromise, the malware fetched its command-and-control (C2) domains from an Ethereum smart contract at runtime, so only the dynamic stage could see them.

lessons.excerpt: libjpeg-turbo 3.x decodes lossless (SOF3) JPEG, but hardwires lossless streams to no scaling — the requested `scale_denom` is silently discarded.

entries.title: CISA KEV: Siemens Software Center DLL search-path flaw CVE-2026-110936 exploited in the wild
entries.takeaway: A local attacker who can drop a DLL where Siemens Software Center looks for one gets code execution; CISA says this is being exploited.
entries.summary: CISA added CVE-2026-110936 in Siemens Software Center to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities list, and an authenticated local attacker can plant a crafted DLL in a searched directory and run code with the application's privileges. Patch it and lock down write access to the application's directories.

lessons.point: The flaw is an uncontrolled DLL search path, which gives local code execution.
lessons.excerpt: an authenticated local attacker to place a specially crafted DLL in a directory that the application searches

entries.title: Abandoned Time4Popcorn updater (CVE-2026-30612) allowed code execution on millions of PCs; researchers disabled it
entries.takeaway: Abandoned software with unsigned updates and lapsed domains is a ready-made supply-chain hole; remove it.
entries.summary: The Time4Popcorn updater fetched executables over HTTP without checking signatures, from an abandoned domain; Eye Security registered the domain and saw up to 3 million Windows and 350,000 macOS clients. They used it to disable the updater, but Android users remain exposed, so uninstall the app.

lessons.point: The article states what control of the update domain would have given an attacker.
lessons.excerpt: Anyone controlling the update domain could manipulate HTTP traffic and execute code as SYSTEM on Windows and as root on macOS.

entries.title: Belarus-aligned Partisan Zmiy hid Vasilek backdoor in VMware Tools for nearly two years in Russian healthcare network
entries.takeaway: Defenders should monitor trusted-but-unwatched directories such as VMware Tools paths, where attackers can hide persistent loaders.
entries.summary: Russian firm Solar says the Partisan Zmiy group (Cyber Partisans) sat in a Russian healthcare organization from early 2024 until discovery in December 2025; the initial access vector is unknown. They used a fake VMware service and a malicious vmtools.dll to run Vasilek 1.5.8.

lessons.point: Solar thinks the group stayed quiet because the access was valuable for espionage and trusted-relationship attacks.
lessons.excerpt: The attacked organization possessed an extensive infrastructure and two-way trusted relationships with numerous subsidiary medical institutions,

entries.title: Eight eMudhra intermediate CA certificates with trivially weak private keys trigger global blocking
entries.takeaway: Update trust stores and bundled root lists everywhere, since anyone holding these keys could mint trusted certificates for any site.
entries.summary: Ars Technica reports that eight eMudhra intermediate certificates had private keys so weak that anyone could issue trusted credentials, and browser makers and some apps and languages have blocked them. Ars reports no malicious use in certificate transparency logs so far; Linux distributions, IoT devices and bundled CLI tools will take a long time to fix, and an attack needs an adversary-in-the-middle position.

lessons.point: The keys were tiny numbers, not real cryptographic keys.
lessons.excerpt: The private key sizes of the compromised keys ranged from 3 to 8 bits.

entries.title: curl moves low and medium severity vulnerability reports to public GitHub from October 26
entries.takeaway: Report floods, including AI-assisted ones, are pushing open source projects to change how they handle vulnerability disclosure.
entries.summary: Maintainer Daniel Stenberg says curl is overwhelmed by vulnerability reports; from October 26, low and medium reports go to the public GitHub repo while high and critical ones stay private. He says over 90 percent of submissions in recent years were judged below HIGH.

lessons.point: Stenberg describes the strain on the project behind the policy change.
lessons.excerpt: We are struggling as a project as all key maintainers feel strained, overloaded and brought to the brink of what we can muster.

entries.title: UpGuard researcher uses OnlyFans copyright takedown data to find hacked university and government sites
entries.takeaway: Cheap search-result monitoring can warn you when your site has been tampered with for SEO spam, which can hide worse access.
entries.summary: UpGuard's Greg Pollock says DMCA takedown requests in Google's transparency report reveal legitimate sites, often .edu and .gov, that were hacked to push adult content in search results; the data is slow, so it is not live detection. He suggests a simple daily search check and basic web hygiene such as CMS updates, and the raw text shows a June 2026 timestamp while the tracker lists 2026-10-19.

lessons.point: Pollock recommends a cheap search-results check as an early warning.
lessons.excerpt: I think having some kind of search engine results monitoring is a pretty cheap, pretty effective way to have an early warning there.
